I don’t think anyone is ever fully qualified when they take on a new project. Regardless of what they’re doing. Alan Yu and I certainly weren’t when we decided to build a robot in our dorm last semester. We were: - first-year engineering students - with little to no design or CAD experience - who had never touched an embedded system - and probably shouldn’t be trusted with electronics in general So why on earth did we want to build a six-legged robot? I could tell you about how I think hardware modularity is the future. I could pitch you on how designs are moving away from big, rigid structures to flexible, plug-and-play components that can be swapped, upgraded or repurposed on the fly. I could walk you through how a modular architecture dramatically shortens iteration cycles, with each component as an independent unit you can test, break, and rebuild without touching the rest. I could even explain to you how that same modularity means swapping out an end effector for a different task—a gripper, a sensor, a drill—takes minutes, not a full redesign. But really, we just thought it would be fun. V1 @ Michigan ’s Product Studio—an incubator where builders take ideas from ‘maybe’ to working product—encouraged us to run with it. We felt that we’d learn a lot from building it, even if it didn’t work. But it worked. Well, sort of. After a few weeks of hard work, we had a moving, modular hexapod robot. As you can imagine, a dorm room isn’t exactly a robotics factory, and our setup was far from perfect. But seeing it actually move… that made every late night, every soldering burn worth it. So next time you have some wild new idea and an itch to build it—you should probably just say yes ;) *pictured below: the bot taking its first steps.*

Incredibly grateful to have been invited as a guest panelist for the Intriciti 2026 Summer Series: On Generations Speaking alongside Dr. Colleen Batchelder (Writer, Forbes) and Jhonnattan Meneses (Boutique Director, Hublot LVMH), we explored how organizations can bridge generational gaps and better understand the expectations, values, and leadership styles of the next generation entering the workforce. As the student representative on the panel, I had the privilege of reflecting on my experiences during my first year at New York University -- from interning at a student-led AI startup to discussing how students navigate mentorship, faith, and career development while living in New York City. We also explored how corporations can create internship experiences that empower Gen Z to contribute beyond traditional work expectations, such as by prioritizing an authentic workplace culture. Thank you to Alana Walker Carpenter , Carter Carpenter , and the Intriciti team for the invitation to have such a thoughtful discussion! #Intriciti2026SummerSeries

Vestris (YC S26) runs the entire real estate closing process. Title insurance is the thorn in the side of every home purchase in America, and almost nobody who buys it can tell you what it does. Behind the scenes, someone is opening emails one at a time as files and paperwork crawl through, manually copying info from pieces of paper. The "modern" software is a decade-old database most small shops can't even afford. So founders Aahil Valliani and Joshua Tang spent months working inside mom-and-pop title shops, closing real files alongside the processors, and built Vestris. It reads every document the moment it lands, pulls county records, drafts the title commitment, and reconciles the closing disclosure. Nothing goes out without a human signing off. Processors are handed a file with the busywork already done, so they can spend their time making judgment calls and the work clients actually remember: walking someone through the biggest purchase of their life. Vestris is already running alongside a shop settling millions in deals a month. Learn more at vestris.ai or reach out at founders@vestris.ai . Congrats on the launch, Aahil and Joshua! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gsMjiUm4

Why create robot intelligence for just one hand, when we could have it learn from many? GEN-1, our latest embodied foundation model, now supports a broad range of end effectors from 5-finger hands, to specialized tools, and everything in between. Each hand is a different sensorimotor interface by which GEN-1 experiences the physical world. Scaling pretraining across thousands of these interfaces teaches GEN-1 a universal physical commonsense that transfers to new hands and new ways to grasp, push, pull, twist, and more. Nature didn’t converge on just a single solution for manipulating the physical world. It exploded into millions. You can see this everywhere in the diversity of life around us: from the beak of a bird, to the trunk of an elephant, from the suction pads of an octopus, to the pollen baskets of a honeybee. The human hand is only a single point in a design space so large we’ve barely begun to map. For machines, five-fingered hands will just be one tool among many; limiting robots to only that would be a failure of imagination. If we can build general intelligence that understands the underlying physics of interaction, then the shape of the hand becomes secondary to the intelligence that drives it. A suction pad, a gripper, a brush, a plasma welding nozzle – are all just different interfaces through which the same intelligence can reshape the physical world. The future of robot hands won’t look like ours. It will look more like a toolbox with a thousand hands: augmented, recombined, and scaled. Robots were always meant to extend what humans can do – to empower people to shape the physical world in places and at scales we never could before. I spent my past weekend competing at the S26 Brookfield Renewable Innovation Challenge in Waterloo - successfully winning the "Best Impact" award. Working with Victor Sabbagh , Ayaan Ghauce , Amyn Aung , and Julian Kapalanga , we combined our strengths to design Waterloos EnerSmart System. Specifically retrofit to the Psychology, Anthropology, and Sociology building (PAS) at Waterloo. Among the features of our design including solar panels, maintenance robots, and sensory HVAC and lighting systems, I was responsible for maximizing the natural light in an otherwise "gloomy" building through innovative architectural and structural concepts - my area of expertise. I began by examining the building's existing floorplans closely, searching for low-cost, high-impact opportunities to brighten the space: • Areas with existing windows: Interior glazing and strategic partitions on non-load-bearing walls to allow daylight to penetrate deeper into the building, supported by light shelves to further distribute light • Deeper, windowless areas (half of the building): Tubular daylight devices (TDDs). More expensive, but a minimally invasive solution to reliably channel natural light across multiple floors while reducing daytime lighting demand My contributions would effectively reduce overall daytime lighting demand and improve the mental health and well-being of students. Our group also accounted for engineering economics, lifecycle cost analysis, greenhouse gas reduction calculations, implementation planning, and return-on-investment modelling. I'm grateful to Brookfield Renewable and the University of Waterloo for an incredible competition, and for the opportunity to learn from Brookfield executives alongside such an amazing team. #BrookfieldRenewable #RenewableEnergy #UniversityofWaterloo

What makes a great engineer? Just over a year ago, if you'd asked me what a software engineer actually does, I couldn't have told you much beyond "they write code." A side effect of growing up in a family with no ties to tech. Last night I visited Palo Alto for the first time. I overheard a conversation between two people (outside of the Amazon office, of all things), and one of them said this: "A great engineer is someone who tries to obsolete themselves. From everything they do." I’m now in a position where I actually work alongside engineers: in my internship and in V1. While I can’t claim to do their jobs, that line feels like a nice guiding principle for almost any kind of work. If I can obsolete myself from a task, automate the mundane parts and hand off the repetitive stuff, then I trust that there’s a better problem waiting for me on the other side. Agree or disagree? p.s. To the guy who drove by with the “10XENGR” license plate, you have my heart
